Title: Rome in World Time, Part 1: Wolves, Kings, and a World in Motion (c. 1000–509 BC)

Summary: Before Rome was an empire or even a republic, it was a cluster of hilltop huts ruled by kings. While those villages grew into a city, Assyria rose and fell, Babylon took Jerusalem, Persia built the largest empire the world had yet seen, Confucius and the Buddha were teaching, and Athens threw out its tyrants within a year of Rome throwing out its last king.

---

This is the first post in a twelve-part series that walks through the entire history of Rome, from the hilltop villages to the fall of Constantinople in 1453, and keeps asking one question: **what else was happening in the world at the same time?**

Most of us learn history in silos. Rome in one class, China in another, the Maya in a documentary we watched once. Putting them side by side produces some genuinely surprising pairings. Rome threw out its last king in the very same years Athens threw out its last tyrant. The Han dynasty was founded in the same year Hannibal lost at Zama. Huns were defeating Romans in Europe and Gupta Indians on the Ganges within a couple of years of each other.

### A note on dates and sources

Dates before about 300 BC are shaky everywhere, not just in Rome. Roman writers like Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus wrote about the regal period roughly 500 years after it happened, and they mixed legend, family propaganda and guesswork. Where a date is traditional or disputed, I flag it with **(trad.)** or **(disputed)**. Each post ends with a short sources list.

## Rome before Rome

Archaeology shows people living on the hills by the Tiber, especially the Palatine, from at least the early first millennium BC. The site had three things going for it: a river crossing (the Tiber Island made fording easy), salt routes running inland from the coast, and defensible hills. Iron Age hut foundations have been found on the Palatine, and the culture of the area is called **Latial** by archaeologists.

These were Latins, one people among many in Italy. To the north were the **Etruscans**, who were richer, more urban and far more sophisticated in this period. To the south, Greeks were planting colonies. Rome began as a small, ambitious village between much bigger neighbours.

## The founding story

Roman tradition says Rome was founded on **21 April 753 BC** by **Romulus**, who killed his twin brother Remus during an argument over the city's walls. The date comes from the scholar Varro, who calculated it in the first century BC. It is a convention, not a fact, but Romans counted years *ab urbe condita* ("from the founding of the city") using it.

The legends are worth knowing because Romans themselves believed them and used them to explain who they were:

- The twins were suckled by a she-wolf after being abandoned on the Tiber.
- Romulus filled his new city with outlaws and refugees, then solved the shortage of women by abducting the daughters of the neighbouring Sabines.
- The Sabine women later threw themselves between their fathers and their Roman husbands to stop the resulting war, and the two peoples merged.

## The seven kings (753–509 BC, trad.)

| King | Traditional reign | What tradition credits him with |
|---|---|---|
| Romulus | 753–716 | Founding, the Senate, the Sabine war |
| Numa Pompilius | 715–673 | Religion, priesthoods, the calendar |
| Tullus Hostilius | 673–642 | War; destruction of Alba Longa |
| Ancus Marcius | 642–617 | Bridge over the Tiber; founding of Ostia |
| Tarquinius Priscus | 616–579 | First Etruscan king; drained the Forum, began big building |
| Servius Tullius | 578–535 | Census, citizen classes, army reform |
| Tarquinius Superbus | 534–509 | Tyranny; Temple of Jupiter; overthrown |

Seven kings over 244 years is too neat, and historians doubt the details. What does seem real is the shape of the story: Rome grew under kings, came under strong **Etruscan influence** in the 600s and 500s BC, and turned into a genuine city. The Forum was drained and paved around the late 600s, the great **Cloaca Maxima** drain was started, and the huge Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus went up on the Capitoline. The **Lapis Niger** inscription in the Forum, from around the 500s BC, mentions a *rex* (king), so kings were real.

### Violence at the top

Even the legends are full of coups. Tarquinius Priscus was murdered by the sons of his predecessor. Servius Tullius was killed in the street by his own son-in-law Tarquinius Superbus and his daughter Tullia, who, the story goes, drove her carriage over her father's body.

## Revolution: the end of the kings (509 BC)

The last king, **Tarquin the Proud**, was overthrown after his son Sextus raped a noblewoman named **Lucretia**, who then took her own life. Her kinsman **Lucius Junius Brutus** led the uprising, the royal family was expelled, and Romans swore never again to have a king. In place of one king they elected **two consuls** for one year each.

This was Rome's founding revolution, and the hatred of the word *rex* that it produced shaped Roman politics for the next 500 years. Julius Caesar was eventually killed partly because people believed he wanted to be king. One of his killers was a Brutus who claimed descent from this one.

Tarquin did not go quietly. He sought help from the Etruscan king **Lars Porsenna** of Clusium, which leads into the stories of Horatius at the bridge (covered in Part 2).

Around 509 BC, according to the Greek historian Polybius, Rome also signed its **first treaty with Carthage**, setting out trading zones. The two cities that would fight to the death 250 years later started as business partners.

## Things you might not have known happened at the same time

**Rome and Athens had their revolutions in the same two years.** Athens expelled its tyrant Hippias in 510 BC and created democracy under Cleisthenes in 508/507. Rome expelled Tarquin in 509. Neither city was copying the other. Both were part of a broader Mediterranean shift away from one-man rule.

**Confucius, the Buddha and Rome's last kings overlapped.** Confucius was teaching in the state of Lu while Servius Tullius and Tarquin the Proud ruled Rome. The Buddha's dates are disputed (scholars argue for about 563–483 BC or about 480–400 BC), but either way he was close in time.

**Persia was the superpower.** When Rome became a republic, the Persian Empire stretched from Egypt and Anatolia to the Indus River. Rome was a small city-state that would not have been worth Darius I's attention.

**Carthage is older than Rome.** By tradition, Carthage was founded about 60 years before Rome and was already a rich trading city when Rome's first king was (supposedly) laying out his walls.

**The kings of Kush ruled Egypt.** In the same decades that Romulus is said to have founded Rome, kings from what is now Sudan ruled as pharaohs over all of Egypt.

## What comes next

Part 2 follows the new Republic as it fights for survival against Etruscans, Latins and hill tribes, gets sacked by Gauls, battles its own poorer citizens in the "Struggle of the Orders", and ends up controlling all of Italy. Meanwhile, Greeks beat Persia at Marathon and Salamis, Alexander the Great conquers to India, and China's Warring States fight their long war.

## Sources and notes

- Livy, *Ab Urbe Condita* (History of Rome), Book 1. The main ancient narrative of the kings. Written c. 27–9 BC, so centuries after the events.
- Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, Books 1–4.
- Polybius, *Histories* 3.22, for the first Rome–Carthage treaty (dated to the first year of the Republic).
- T. J. Cornell, *The Beginnings of Rome* (1995). The standard modern account of early Rome and the reliability of the traditions.
- Mary Beard, *SPQR: A History of Ancient Rome* (2015), chapters 2–3.
- Herodotus, *Histories*, for Persia, Lydia and the Athenian tyrants.
- Overview: [Founding of Rome (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_of_Rome) and [Roman Kingdom (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Kingdom).

**Flags:** The 753 BC founding date, the seven kings and their reign lengths are traditional and not reliable as history. Dates for David, the Buddha and Jimmu are traditional or disputed. The Olympic date of 776 BC comes from later Greek lists. Dates for the Assyrian, Babylonian and Persian events are much more secure, because they come from contemporary records.
